title: CDC — Measles Cases and Outbreaks (United States)

chunks.text:
Source: https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html (data feed https://www.cdc.gov/wcms/vizdata/measles/measles_hosp.json), retrieved 2026-08-11.
As of the latest CDC update, a total of 2,465 confirmed measles cases were reported in the United States in 2026. There have been 0 confirmed deaths from measles in 2026.
As of the latest CDC update, a total of 2,289 confirmed measles cases were reported in the United States in 2025. There were 3 confirmed deaths from measles in 2025.
Note: this custom scraper renders the CDC measles JSON data feed into compact HTML because the page's case/death figures are injected client-side and are absent from the statically served table cells. Counts are cumulative year-to-date totals.

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, which affects mostly children. It is transmitted via droplets from the nose, mouth, or throat of infected persons. Initial symptoms, which usually appear 10-12 days after infection, include high fever, runny nose, bloodshot eyes, and tiny white spots on the inside of the mouth. Several days later, a rash develops, starting on the face and upper neck and gradually spreading downwards.
There is no specific treatment for measles and most people recover within 2-3 weeks. However, particularly in malnourished children and people with reduced immunity, measles can cause serious complications, including blindness, encephalitis, severe diarrhea, ear infection, and pneumonia. Measles can be prevented by immunization.
• Measles is a very contagious viral disease that especially affects children and can cause severe health problems, including severe diarrhea, ear infections, blindness, pneumonia, and encephalitis (swelling of the brain). Some of these complications can lead to death.
• At the global level, measles continues to be one of the leading causes of death among young children, despite the fact that there is a safe and effective vaccine to prevent it. There is no specific antiviral treatment against the measles virus.
• Serious cases are especially frequent in malnourished young children, especially those whose immune systems are weakened. In populations with high levels of malnutrition and inadequate health care, measles can kill in up to 10% of cases.
• Measles is transmitted by airborne droplets from the nose, mouth, or throat of an infected person. The virus can stay active and contagious in the air or on surfaces for two hours.
• Symptoms tend to be high fever, runny nose, cough, red and watery eyes, small white spots on the inside of the cheeks, and widespread rash all over the body.
• Before widespread vaccination began in 1980, measles caused 2.6 million deaths a year throughout the world, 12,000 of them in the Americas.
• Between 1970 and 1979, Latin American countries reported about 220,000 cases of measles a year.

title: US sees highest number of measles cases in 35 years

chunks.text:
The US has hit a 35-year high in measles cases, according to new figures from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The US has seen 2,318 confirmed cases of measles in 2026, just seven months into the year, up from last year's high of 2,289, when two unvaccinated children died of the disease.
The rising number of cases have come as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates.
In November, a panel is set to decide whether the US will lose its status of having eliminated measles, which Canada lost last year.
A country loses elimination status after a year or more of continuous transmission of the same strain of the measles virus.
The US has recorded more measles cases over the past 18 months than the total number over 25 years before that.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.
Last year, an outbreak among the Mennonite community in Texas killed two unvaccinated children, and an unvaccinated adult in neighbouring New Mexico.
Over the past month, Virginia and Pennsylvania have been dealing with new measles outbreaks, while the state of Utah is still responding to a cluster of infections that began last year.
Some 45 states have recorded cases.
Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has been criticised by public health experts who argue his remarks and remaking of US vaccine policy has hindered efforts to stop the outbreaks.
A vaccine skeptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which has been proven safe and effective.
The US recommends two shots to children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.
He has stated that the MMR vaccine is the "most effective way to prevent the spread of measles" but has also promoted unproven treatments.
Earlier this year, he told lawmakers that a several countries have recently lost their measles elimination status, and defended the response by US officials.
"The whole world had their worst measles year," he said.
Earlier this year, a federal judge blocked the US government from implementing a series of sweeping changes to childhood immunisations under Kennedy's leadership, including slashing the number of recommended shots for children from 17 to 11.
To achieve herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects the unvaccinated, around 95% of the population must have the shots. But vaccination rates have dipped far below that in some areas.
Last year, during an outbreak among the Russian and Ukrainian immigrant community in Spartanburg, South Carolina, some schools in the community had vaccination rates as low as 20%.

title: Map: Track the spread of measles in the U.S.

chunks.text:
Measles, one of the most contagious viruses in the world, is regularly infecting people in the U.S. again.
Already in 2026 more than 2,300 cases have been counted, making 2026 the two year for measles infections in the U.S. since 2000.
NBC News is continuing to track confirmed measles cases across the United States, using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data.
Measles case counts reached a 34-year high last year, and seven months into 2026, this year’s total is even higher.
The disease epicenter at the start of the year was in South Carolina, where the CDC has confirmed 600-plus measles cases. As of late January, more than 500 people were in quarantine and hundreds infected in the state. State officials declared the South Carolina outbreak over in April.
The map below will be updated regularly to show year-to-date new measles case counts reported in each state and Washington, D.C.
Measles infection counts skyrocketed last year with 2,289 confirmed cases, which had been the most reported since 1991. This comes despite the virus being marked as being “eliminated” in the U.S. —a designation meaning it is no longer constantly circulating — in 2000. The U.S. is in danger of losing that status following a year of continuous spread of the disease.
Three people, including two young girls, died in the U.S. from measles last year.
The major outbreaks last year began with West Texas in February. In October, a measles outbreak occurred along the Utah and Arizona border. In all, the CDC recorded 48 measles outbreaks in 2025, up from 16 in 2024. So far in 2026, 35 measles outbreaks have been reported.
Childhood vaccination rates have been backsliding, leaving communities vulnerable to this deadly disease.
The measles vaccine was introduced in 1963, marking a turning point for the contagious disease, which used to infect hundreds of thousands and kill thousands in the country every year.
CORRECTION (Feb. 20, 2026, 3:57 p.m. ET): A previous version of a graphic in this article miscalculated the relative size of this year's measles case count. As of Feb. 20, this year's case count is four times the size of 2025's at the same point in the year, and 25 times the size of 2024's at the same point, not seven times and 30 times higher.

title: US measles cases hit 2,318 in 2026, surpassing last year's total: CDC

chunks.text:
This marks the highest number of cases recorded since 1991.
The number of confirmed measles cases in the U.S. so far this year has hit 2,318, surpassing the total reported for all last year, according to data updated Friday from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Previously, last year's total of 2,289 was the highest number of recorded measles cases in more than 30 years, CDC data shows. The new figure marks the highest number of cases recorded since 1991.
Cases have been confirmed in 43 states and the District of Columbia. Sixteen of this year's total have been among international visitors to the U.S., according to the CDC.
The majority of measles cases in 2026 have been confirmed among children and teenagers aged 19 and younger, according to the CDC. About one in 10 children under age 5 have been hospitalized.
About 93% of cases are among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, CDC data shows.
Meanwhile, 3% of cases are among those who have received just one dose of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine and 4% of cases are among those who received the recommended two doses, according to the CDC.
"Crossing this threshold is a tragic reminder that measles has made an alarming comeback in the United States," Dr. Richard Besser, former acting CDC director during the Obama administration, said in a statement to ABC News. "As a pediatrician and a parent, it breaks my heart that so many children are suffering needlessly from a dangerous and potentially fatal disease that vaccines can prevent. It represents a profound moral failure on the part of our national health leaders."
The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective, and two doses are 97% effective against measles, the CDC says.
However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2024 to 2025 school year, 92.5% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 92.7% seen in the previous school year and the 95.2% seen in the 2019 to 2020 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Some public health specialists previously told ABC News they believe the U.S. is on track to lose the elimination status it earned in 2000.
The specialists said there are several reasons for the U.S. breaking measles case records for the second year in a row, including declining vaccination rates, people not fearing the measles virus, a loss of trust in public health institutions and a perceived lack of clear guidance and communication from the nation's top public health officials.
